subject: Quantifying effective amount of data imposed by prior

messages.author: 885539f3f5ae8fd5
messages.subject: Quantifying effective amount of data imposed by prior
parts:
Hi,

We just used stan in a Monte Carlo simulation study to look at the effects of sample size, number of items, prior (mis)specification, and data (non)normality, in recovering the intraclass correlation parameter. I'm attaching a sample stan script in case it helps clarify my question. Now, one of my colleagues asked if we could use stan to "quantify the effective amount of data imposed by the prior" in some of the conditions, and whether this was something stan could do automatically. I frankly have no idea what this means, and upon clarification he wrote "if the sample size is 100, approximately how many additional pseudo-observations does a prior include?".

So my question is how can I use stan to get this information? Is this something I can extract from the fitted model object using R? (I used rstan.) And... I dread this part, but I only saved the results of one replication per unique combination of experimental conditions (sample size, number of items, data distribution, etc.) for the sake of saving space. Am I going to have to refit all replications to get this information from every replication? Or is this something that will be constant across all replications of a given set of conditions (i.e., only affected by the experimental conditions, not by the randomness in the data)?

Sorry for how basic these questions are, but I am very much a Bayes novice and just happen to be the only person on this project who even knows how to start up stan in R!!

- Jonathan

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Quantifying effective amount of data imposed by prior
parts:
The exponential family priors can all be viewed as prior data.
You can just inspect them to see how much prior data they represent.
For instance, a Beta(alpha,beta) density has (alpha + beta - 2) prior
observations. If you have a uniform prior for a bernoulli observation
and have N successes and M failures, the posterior is Beta(1 + N, 1 + M).

I'm not sure how to calculate for other exponential family priors or for
non-exponential family densities (or even if the latter makes sense).

See: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjugate_prior#Pseudo-observations

Apparently the Wikipedia author knew about as much as me, but not more!

- Bob
